newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Catalans step up pressure on government.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Catalans step up pressure on government.

text.p: Catalan nationalists, whose support is vital to the Spanish government's parliamentary majority, intensified pressure on the ruling party on Tuesday to win concessions for their region.

Jordi Pujol, leader of the Catalan coalition Convergence and Unity, has pledged his support for Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's centre-right Popular Party (PP) government at least until mid-1998 when Spain hopes to enter European monetary and economic union.
But his pledge belies deep strains in the uneasy alliance between the conservative ruling party and its key ally that could tear it apart once the single European currency is launched.
Catalan officials made clear on Tuesday their support was in no way guaranteed beyond next year.

"I feel absolutely uncomfortable with Convergence and Unity support for the PP and I don't think my colleagues in the coalition feel comfortable either," Catalan parliamentarian Josep Lopez de Lerma told a Catalan radio station on Tuesday.
Lerma and other party officials raised concerns after a Spanish television network executive alleged last week that an aide to Aznar had threatened him with imprisonment.
Aznar's minority government counts on the Catalans to muster a majority in parliament but Lerma warned last week the party may pull its support over the alleged threats.

At the same time, Convergence and Unity, which is the main power broker in the autonomous region of Catalonia, is also stepping up pressure to wring concessions from the government for its regional interests.

The Catalans want more funding for regional health services and wider official recognition of the Catalan language. In addition, the two parties are at loggerheads over exclusive television rights for soccer broadcasts.

"The commitment is to support the government until the entry into European monetary union," said a senior Catalan official who asked not to be named. "When that is done, if these other issues are not resolved, we will have to reconsider."
The Catalans effectively brought down the previous Socialist government, headed by Felipe Gonzalez, when they withdrew their backing over mounting scandals.
The crisis atmosphere seemed to have dissipated after Aznar met Pujol on Friday for a lengthy one-on-one discussion.
Pujol had urgently demanded that meeting after the head of Spain's Antenna 3 network Antonio Asenino alleged an Aznar aide had threatened in a phone call to send him to jail.
He said the call came after he abandoned a government-backed digital TV consortium and joined rival media conglomerate Grupo Prisa, taking soccer television broadcast rights with him.

The opposition Socialist party, headed by Gonzalez, proposed on Tuesday a parliamentary investigation into "abuses of power" by the ruling party in its dealings with companies affiliated with Grupo Prisa.

Even after the Aznar-Pujol meeting, Catalans' concerns were reawakened when the television executive Asensio named the aide who allegedly threatened him as chief government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez.
"I'm horrified and stunned by the threats Miguel Angel Rodriguez made against Asensio," Lerma said.
Rodriguez denied the allegations on Tuesday.
"I never threatened any media executive. I never threatened any journalist," he told reporters.
Rodriguez said Asensio's allegations were originally put forth by the Socialists.
